cs.t: Agreed. I have used a HP N40L ProLiant MicroServer since 2013 as home NAS and Time Machine backups via samba. Rock solid hardware, incredibly expandable, and today runs FreeBSD 15.1 with ZFS. Additional hardware modifications include; CD-ROM replaced by two 3.5" HDDs on mounts (now six HDDs of 10TB each in ZRAID1), a SAS card to add two mirrored bootable SSDs underneath CD-ROM drive space, a 2x 2.5G NIC (limited to 4GB/s slot) for dedicated NFS link, while additional internal SATA and external SATA ports unused. Next: replace PSU fan with quieter Noctua fan.
cs.th: How to Build a Minimal ZFS NAS Without Synology, QNAP, TrueNAS

cs.t: Many of us are sysadmins at home. Home Assistant, home NAS, home DVRs, etc. Consumer NASes are in tension against the DIY hacker / homelab people who often run these things. These NASes are just complicated enough to be consumer unfriendly, but not enough for "our" needs. The author has a good point about how NAS hardware is more integrated - less capable for power users - while the software has stagnated into a sort of semi embedded, minimal viable product. Just yesterday I heard about a friend-of-a-friend type situation where the sysadmin husband was in hospice, and the wife was struggling to figure out how to operate the NAS to recover family photos, etc. I think consumer NAS manufacturers could add a "foolproof backup connection method," such as a USB port in USB device mode, so the NAS could be easily connected to a laptop by someone with little computer knowledge, in read-only mode. That said, my home NAS is "the littlest server": an aging ProLiant DL380 Gen8 MicroServer. It's behind a double conversion UPS. SAS card + drives, Proxmox running virtualized FreeNAS, etc. Typical overdone geek build. I have not seen a finer NAS platform for the precocious home admin. I wish there were newer versions which kept the enterprise style "lights out management," and added m.2 and such, but I think HP Enterprise as a company is not interested in the homelab use case.

cs.t: I got a gen10 plus microserver and liked it so much that I got a second one. Throw FreeBSD on it and add a couple lines to /etc/exports and rc.conf and it's a NAS right out of the box

cs.t: I'd love to be able to get a specced down, "low"-power, version of this to use as a home server: - lower-end cpu (the 32-core version would be just fine for me) - keeping the possibilty having lot of ram around (128gb? 256gb? 512gb?) - low-end gpu or no gpu at all (it would be headless anyway) - keep the ipmi around - maybe some 4 hot-swappable 3.5" drive bays ? I could see myself blowing 2000-3000$ on something like as long as I can keep it working for ten years. Maybe update it a bit over the years. And i'm not joking about the ten-years: I'm still using a 2014-era HP MicroServer Gen8 and it works great. It shows its age, but it does still work great.

cs.t: HP Microserver Gen8 with: > Debian 8 > Xeon E3-1260L > 12 GB RAM > 120GB SSD (OS), 2 x 3TB WD RED (Data), 2 x 4TB HGST (Movies/TV Shows) > Plex (Movies, TV Shows, Music, Photos) > CouchPotato (Movie Downloading) > Transmission (Torrents) > CrashPlan (backups) > Raspberry Pi Camera Streams (samba share) > + more stuff All these applications run in their own docker containers. I used to do local web development in a virtual machine, now it all sits on this server. Love it and it works 'magically'. Connected to the TV is a Quad-core android TV Box.
cs.th: Ask HN: What is your home media PC setup?

cs.t: I've spent a lot of time thinking about this... I don't trust Drobo/Synology etc because if the unit dies I need another one to retrieve my data. Jungledisk adds up if you have 100+GB, Backblaze is the best of these services, however they are proprietary, and imagine if either were cracked and your life ended up on on a torrent server somewhere... In the end I decided upon a HP Microserver running Ubuntu with disks in RAID5 + a cheap UPS. I then have an rsync cronjob on my laptop. I tried FreeNAS but it was slow. I may consider an offsite backup of the Ubuntu server (critical files (photos etc)) to AWS with Duplicity and PGP... So far I feel the safest and happiest I've been in awhile about my backup situation.
cs.th: Ask HN: How do you Backup your Personal Files?
